papers_read.title_as_printed: Mild Cognitive Impairment detection based on EEG and HRV data (Boudaya, Chaabene, Bouaziz, Hoekelmann, Chaari; Digit Signal Process 2024)
Development of a Machine Learning Model to Discriminate Mild Cognitive Impairment Subjects from Normal Controls in Community Screening (Jiang et al.; Brain Sci 2022)

what_each_reports.P-83: 15 participants (Magdeburg; 8 MCI, 7 HC after excluding 9 of 24), 14-channel Emotiv EEG + Polar HRV recorded during CERAD sub-tests, features from 3-s signal windows, 75/25 shuffled split of windows; hybrid SVM/GB/RF voting: average accuracy over seven CERAD tests 93.86% (sens 93.87%, spec 93.53%), best test T1 97.43%; 10-fold 95.23% and LOOCV 96.14% for T1 (Tables 7-8). Re-implementing Jiang et al. [93] (= P-214) on its own data gives 87.68% average (Table 9).
what_each_reports.P-214: Shanghai community screening: Cohort 1 (336 subjects) for training with 5-fold CV and Cohort 2 (92 subjects, another district) as an independent test; features = 1-electrode EEG + eye tracking + 20-subtest neuropsychological battery + demographics, MRMR selection, RBF SVM: accuracy 84.5 +/- 4.43% (AUC 0.942) in Cohort 1 and 88.8 +/- 3.59% (AUC 0.966) in Cohort 2 (Tables 3-4).

quantity_a: Accuracy of classifying 3-second EEG+HRV signal windows (window level, windows of the same 15 people shuffled across train and test) as MCI vs HC during a CERAD cognitive task, averaged over seven sub-tests.
quantity_b: Subject-level accuracy of classifying community-dwelling older adults as MCI vs NC from EEG, eye tracking and neuropsychological test scores, in 5-fold CV on 336 subjects (84.5%) and on an independent 92-subject cohort (88.8%).
incompatible_if_same: No. Each paper reports its own method's score. The only ordering claim is P-83's, that its hybrid model beats a re-implementation of P-214's pipeline on P-83's 15-subject data (93.86% vs 87.68%); P-214 makes no claim about P-83's method or data, so nothing is refuted.

gates.task: match: MCI vs healthy controls detection (T1).
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: German 15-subject lab sample vs two Shanghai community cohorts; the record's dataset_equal 'Yes' reflects both registry rows being 'not reported', not a shared dataset. No waiver.
gates.validation_tier: mismatch: P-83 uses window-level random splits and CV within 15 people; P-214 adds a subject-disjoint independent cohort from a different district (Cohort 2).
gates.modality_family: mismatch in part: both use EEG, but P-83 adds heart-rate variability while P-214 adds eye tracking and a 20-subtest neuropsychological battery, which on its own reaches 75% accuracy.

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: P-83's accuracy is over signal windows (its T1 confusion matrix counts 34 TP and 39 TN from a 25% split of windows of 15 people), P-214's is over subjects. A window-level accuracy with the same person on both sides of the split is not the same estimand as subject-level accuracy.
performance_validity: The automatic test is not tripped by the 93.86% average, but P-83 meets the substance of the exclusion: 15 subjects, internal validation only with window-level shuffling, best sub-test 97.43% and LOOCV 96.14%. A performance comparison resting on it could not be genuine in any case.
independence: Distinct studies, cohorts and authors. P-83 cites and re-implements P-214 ([93]).
grounds: The estimands differ: P-83 reports window-level accuracy with windows from the same 15 people in training and test, whereas P-214 reports subject-level accuracy, including on an independent cohort.
The dataset-family and validation-tier gates fail and the predictor sets differ (EEG+HRV vs EEG+eye tracking+neuropsychological battery), with no waiver on record.

The only cross-study ordering, P-83's re-implementation of P-214's method on P-83's data, is not contradicted by anything P-214 reports; and P-83's 15-subject, internally validated, near-ceiling result falls under the performance-validity exclusion in substance.

evidence_quotes.quote: Our dataset includes 15 subjects who were randomly assigned to training and testing groups of 7 HC and 8 MCI, respectively.

For each test, we separated our data into 75% for the training set and 25% for the testing set. To boost the effectiveness of ML model accuracy and to reduce the rate of overfitting, we applied the shuffling strategy throughout the data partitioning process.
Based on the first test, Fig. 5 presents the confusion matrix results using the hybrid ML model, where the corresponding TP and TN classified sets are 34 and 39.
With our dataset, we put these methods into practice. For each CERAD test, the comparison between our suggested method and these works is shown in Table 9.
We found that the classification accuracy of the proposed model achieved 84.5 +/- 4.43% and 88.8 +/- 3.59% in Cohort 1 and Cohort 2, respectively.
Cohort 2 was used as an independent test group to verify the robustness of the classification results.

record_defects: claim_a still reads 'P-322: Acc 93.87'; after the 2026-08-30 repoint the paper is P-83, whose accuracy is 93.86% (93.87% is its sensitivity).
dataset_equal 'Yes' is wrong: the two studies use unrelated cohorts (Magdeburg lab sample vs Shanghai communities).
modality_family 'eeg_meg' omits that P-83 adds HRV and P-214 adds eye tracking and neuropsychological test scores.
The record does not note that P-214 also reports 88.8% on an independent cohort, or that P-83 re-implemented P-214's method on its own data (87.68%).
P-214 itself is internally inconsistent on cohort composition (abstract '184 MCI patients and 152 NC'; Section 3.1 '152 MCI patients and 184 normal controls').
what_would_change_the_verdict: Subject-level, subject-disjoint accuracy from P-83 on a cohort of comparable size and the same feature family would be needed to set the two against each other; even then, differing method scores without a refuted ordering would be a false positive.
